questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Study the diagram below showing the four positions of the earth during revolution round the sun and:

![fig-1](gce-ol-geography-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

(i) State: - the dates lettered A to D and
- the seasons numbered i to iv
(ii) Briefly describe TWO proofs to show that the earth is spherical

(4 + 4 = 8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The dates A to D and the seasons i to iv (4 marks).**

*How the diagram is read.* The arrows on the orbit show that the Earth moves from A to B, then C, then D, and back to A. The Sun is at the centre of the orbit (not drawn). The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees and always points in the same direction in space. In position **B** the north end of the axis (N) leans towards the Sun, so the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun (the Tropic of Cancer gets the overhead sun): this is the **June solstice**. In position **D** the north end leans away from the Sun: **December solstice**. At **A** and **C** the axis leans neither towards nor away from the Sun, so day and night are equal: these are the **equinoxes**; because the Earth goes from D to A, A is after the December solstice (**21 March**) and C is after the June solstice (**23 September**).

| Position | Date | Overhead sun | Season in the northern hemisphere | Numeral |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 21 March (March equinox) | Equator | **spring** (autumn in the southern hemisphere) | i |
| D | 22 December (December solstice) | Tropic of Capricorn | **winter** (summer in the southern hemisphere) | ii |
| C | 23 September (September equinox) | Equator | **autumn** (spring in the southern hemisphere) | iii |
| B | 21 June (June solstice) | Tropic of Cancer | **summer** (winter in the southern hemisphere) | iv |

*Answer:* A = 21 March, B = 21 June, C = 23 September, D = 22 December; seasons i = spring, ii = winter, iii = autumn, iv = summer (northern hemisphere). The dates may vary by one day from year to year (20 or 21 March, 21 or 22 June, 22 or 23 September, 21 or 22 December).

**(ii) Two proofs that the earth is spherical (4 marks, 2 marks each).**

1. **Circumnavigation (travelling round the earth).** Ships and aircraft that keep going in one direction (for example the expedition begun by Magellan in 1519 and completed by his crew in 1522, and every round-the-world flight today) come back to the point from which they left without turning back and without falling off an edge. This is possible only on a curved, closed surface such as a sphere.
2. **The earth's shadow in a lunar eclipse.** During an eclipse of the moon the shadow of the earth that crosses the moon always has a **curved, circular edge**, whatever the position of the earth. Only a sphere always casts a round shadow (a disc seen edge-on would sometimes give a straight shadow).

*Other proofs that can be used:* a ship coming from the sea appears **hull last** as it goes over the horizon (the mast is seen first when it approaches and disappears last when it leaves); photographs of the earth taken from space by satellites and astronauts; the difference in time between places (when it is noon in Douala it is not noon in London) and the change of the altitude of the Pole Star with latitude.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Draw a well labeled diagram of the hydrological cycle

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **hydrological cycle** (water cycle) is the continuous movement of water between the sea, the atmosphere and the land. It is driven by the **energy of the Sun** and by gravity. A well drawn and labelled diagram (6 marks) should show the following.

![fig-2](gce-ol-geography-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_2.png)

**Labels expected (1 mark each, up to 6):**

1. **Evaporation** of water from the sea, lakes and rivers (arrows going up).
2. **Transpiration** from plants (and evaporation from the soil; together they are called evapotranspiration).
3. **Condensation** of the water vapour into **clouds** as the air rises and cools; the wind carries the moisture inland.
4. **Precipitation** (rain, snow or hail) falling on the sea and on the land.
5. **Surface run-off** (overland flow) towards the river, then **river flow** to the sea.
6. **Infiltration** into the soil, **percolation** through the rock and **groundwater flow** (below the **water table**) towards the sea, the **sun** as the source of energy, and the sea as the final store.

*Presentation:* give the diagram a title, use arrows to show the direction of movement, and write the labels neatly next to the arrows. The cycle is **closed**: the water that falls on the land returns to the sea, and the sea supplies the atmosphere again. In Cameroon, for example, heavy rain on the slopes of Mount Cameroon and on the western highlands feeds rivers that return to the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Define any TWO of the following:
food chain ; soil profile ; biomas

(2 + 2 = 4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any two of the three definitions earn full marks (2 marks each). All three are given here.

- **Food chain:** a **sequence of living organisms** in an ecosystem in which each one is **eaten by the next** and which shows the **transfer of food energy** from one organism to another. It begins with a producer (a green plant) and goes through consumers, for example **grass, then grasshopper, then bird, then hawk** (or grass, cattle, man).
- **Soil profile:** a **vertical section through the soil**, from the surface down to the parent rock, which shows the **different layers (horizons)** of the soil, for example the humus and topsoil (A horizon), the subsoil (B horizon), the weathered parent material (C horizon) and the bedrock; the layers differ in colour, texture and composition.
- **Biome** (printed "biomas" in the paper): a **large natural community of plants and animals** that covers a very wide area of the earth and is controlled mainly by **climate**, so that the vegetation and the animal life are similar over the whole area, for example the tropical rainforest, the savanna (tropical grassland) or the hot desert.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) You have studied weather elements and instruments used in measuring them. In which domains can this knowledge be put to use.

(2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Knowledge of weather elements (temperature, rainfall, humidity, pressure, wind, sunshine) and of the instruments used to measure them (thermometer, rain gauge, hygrometer, barometer, anemometer and wind vane, sunshine recorder) is used in many **domains** (any two, 1 mark each, with a short example):

- **Agriculture:** choosing the planting and harvesting dates, deciding when to irrigate or to spray, and protecting crops against frost, drought or storms.
- **Air and sea transport:** pilots and ship captains use wind, visibility and storm forecasts for safe take-off, landing and navigation; fishermen decide when it is safe to go to sea.
- **Weather forecasting and disaster management:** warnings about floods, storms and drought help to protect lives and property.
- **Construction and public works:** planning roads, bridges and buildings according to rainfall and wind.
- **Tourism, health, energy and daily life:** choosing the best season for tourism, preventing diseases linked with the weather, producing solar or wind energy, and deciding what to wear or what activities to plan.
